install.effects: Frozen pinned dependency installation; no setup, global changes or deployment.

setup.effects: Build, migrate, prepare private settings and the native first owner; stop the temporary app.

dev.effects: Foreground app with assets/HMR, health-gated readiness and automatic local owner entry.

preview.effects: Serve fixed production output, preserve local owner and durable state, stop after idle timeout or explicit stop.

verify.effects: Run the complete nonrecursive verification target.

reset.effects: Explicitly confirmed deletion of the contained local inventory; no remote effect.

deploy.effects: Owner-account provision, migration, publication and health. Today pinned rer 0.2.77 dry-run combines local validation/build with credentialed read-only Cloudflare GETs for the account Workers subdomain and the Worker settings and secret names (three GETs for an existing Worker); refuses without credentials or a required secret neither held nor supplied, validates supplied private mail inputs, sends no mail and changes no provider resources. The required zero-outbound dry-run and separately started provider preflight are not yet built or proved; see OPERATIONS.md.

export.effects: Export the local copy with --output, or run the declared hosted-export argv with --target remote. Hosted output keeps the seed's own format; the summary names its path and exit status.

import.effects: Confirmed validated atomic restore into an empty local destination; native identities retained.

demo.effects: A throwaway demo of this seed (rer dev --demo): fresh data in .rer/demo/START (deleted when it stops: --stop, Ctrl-C or its end, one hour by default or --idle-timeout), the saved owner signed in through the demo persona, a separate RER_OWNER_OPEN link for single-use native owner entry on loopback (15-minute expiry; never saved), the seed's demo data, Demo in the app name and title, real public reads/checks and simulated external writes (RER_DEMO=1; the checkout's own data is never touched).

adopt-edition.effects: Add edition.json and sources.lock.json for the existing tracked local source, preserving declared project identity and existing copy/composition records. Create an empty base-copies.json only when none exists. Review and stage the new authoring inputs; no source regeneration, install setup or commit.

refresh-base.effects: Consent to each declared edition edit with repeatable --edition-migration ID; refresh leaves the edit owed. Refresh recorded Base copies to --ref FULL_COMMIT, preserving acknowledged adaptations and applied migrations; announce removed singleton retirement. Deliver invoked workflow helpers atomically; adopt tracked known historical Verify templates and preserve divergent workflows with adoption notices. Acquire committed source from the declared Base repository (default https://github.com/runeditrun/base.git), or read immutable trees, blobs and ancestry through authenticated gh with --from-api, or use --base CHECKOUT or --base-archive DIRECTORY with --ref FULL_COMMIT for an exported source tree. --offline requires --base or --base-archive and never acquires remote source. Refuse incomplete Git checkouts without changing their records. Review the diff and run edition tests before committing.

signin.effects: A one-time sign-in link for the hosted owner, without mail. Uses the Cloudflare credentials that deployed --environment (default production; from the environment or --env-file) to write a single-use grant for the recorded owner into that deployment's auth database, then prints the link once to this terminal; it is never saved. The link works once, only for that owner, expires within 15 minutes, and its use is recorded in the owner's audit log. Signed in this way, the owner can correct a wrong email in settings.

size.effects: Statement size against D1's limits, measured in SQLite on this computer with no account or network. D1 refuses a statement at 100 FROM items, counted with every CTE and view reference expanded in place, or at expression depth 100, and local SQLite and Miniflare accept both; rer fails at 90 of either, a margin of 10 because D1 changed how it enforces them without notice on 10 Nov 2026. With no flags it checks every view and trigger statement of the build's D1 migrations (dist/server/wrangler.json). --migrations DIR checks the objects of that migrations directory instead of the build's. --statements FILE checks the statements of FILE ({"statements":[{"name","sql"}]}, the fleet runner's format) against that schema. Each failure is named with both numbers and the start of its SQL. Exit 1 if any statement fails, 0 if none, 3 with no build and no --migrations. --json lists every statement as {name, fromItems, depth, ok}. With a size-check.json at the checkout root (or --declaration FILE, a declaration kept outside it), rer then builds the declared shape at a small and a large size, each in its own disposable local D1 install served as the hosted check serves the build: the owner is signed in with the bootstrap agent-door conformance uses (the setup manifest's owner-claim step, else verification.owner), each table is generated inside D1 by chunked INSERT … SELECT so the schema's own triggers fire, and each declared table is read back. It prints, for each size and table, the declared count, the count read back and the time per phase; a generation error names the size, the table, the row range, SQLite's message and its column, exits 1 and prints no built line for that size. budget.timeoutSeconds bounds both sizes and a timeout names the phase. While it serves installs it takes verify's job-queue slot (--no-queue only in the original CI environment). Then the personas sign in and every declared flow runs on each size, small first, through a rows-read meter wrapped around the Worker's D1 bindings (fetch, scheduled, queue, Durable Objects and waitUntil work; queues are held and queue consumer work is not measured). A flow fails when it reads more rows at large than its ceiling, more at large than at small by over growthPercent of small plus growthRows (unless growth.allowed), answers the wrong status, has a statement refused or failed by local D1, or runs a statement at 90 FROM items or depth; each failure names its rule and the three statements that read the most rows at large. --json carries every flow at both sizes; --write-statements DIR writes small.json and large.json in the fleet runner's statements format. --statements runs the statement check alone. rer verify runs the schema-object check as its last step.

# Source structure and contact erasure

Before any contact erasure, incomplete uploads can be reviewed with explicit
omissions or rejections. At upload, every key and scalar value in the parts the
readers do not interpret is hashed whole, as an email (trimmed, lower case), an
external ID and a source ID, into a private index stored beside the original.
Erasing a contact removes an incomplete upload's private originals, extracted
files, plans and journals when its understood identities or that index hold
one of the erased contact's identities or known aliases. Other people's
uploads keep their custody. An incomplete upload without an index (older
custody, or an upload interrupted before its index was stored) is still fenced
by any erasure in its workspace. After any contact erasure, incomplete new
uploads are refused before private bytes are admitted. Matching is by whole
value only: the importer does not search inside text for email addresses,
whether in uninterpreted fields or in message, article, saved-reply, title or
name strings. Understood primitive text retains the documented mapping and
erasure behavior.

| Record or container | Structural checks |
| --- | --- |
| All supported records | Source ID, type/kind strings and original timestamps; every additional field is classified. |
| Zendesk users | Name/email/external ID strings, role string, string tag array; custom fields are opaque. |
| Intercom contacts | Optional name/email/external ID strings; tag list object and each tag's ID/name/type; custom fields are opaque. A supplied non-null name of another type rejects contact mapping. |
| Zendesk tickets | Requester and optional assignee IDs, status/subject, string tag array, comments array, optional via object. |
| Zendesk comments | ID, author ID, explicit boolean visibility, original timestamp and string body/plain body. Attachment and metadata values are opaque. |
| Zendesk via | Channel string; source routing metadata is opaque. A malformed channel rejects conversation mapping. |
| Intercom conversations | Channel object, contact-list object and every participant, source object, parts-list object and every part, tag-list object, optional assignment IDs, state/title/subject. |
| Intercom source/parts | IDs, type/part-type strings, string bodies/subjects, part timestamps, author objects; attachments are opaque. Unknown fields on the source, part or list container are independently reported. |
| Recorded Intercom people | ID, optional type/name/email/external ID strings for participants and source/part authors, including historical staff. Known email and external aliases are linked to the source ID even if mapping rejects the conversation. |
| Zendesk macros | Title, timestamps, action array and each action's field/value. Reply values must be strings. Public-mode values must be booleans or the strings `true`/`false`. Other workflow action values and restrictions are opaque and never activated. |
| Intercom macros | Name, string HTML/plain body representations, ISO timestamps, visibility string, string channel array. Dynamic content remains rejected. |
| Articles | Title/body/publication values and timestamps; Zendesk audience-ID arrays check each ID. Intercom Markdown alternatives are string typed. Audience rules, translations, article tag/availability/scheduling metadata are opaque. Section/parent IDs are checked as IDs. |
| Derived tags | String names and understood common fields. Standalone vendor tag inventories remain unsupported. |
| Intercom envelopes | Known record collections, list-type string and numeric total count. Empty/null pagination objects contain no identity; nonempty pagination and malformed metadata become located unsupported decisions. |

Both supplied discriminators must be nonempty strings and must agree. Conflicting
or malformed discriminators are refused before private custody, with the exact
source line and JSON pointer. A list discriminator with a source `id` is ambiguous
and is refused. True list envelopes and untyped convenience collections accept
arrays; a null, scalar or object in a collection position is refused. JSONL lines
use the same lowering as JSON documents. Arrays and envelopes contain records,
not nested envelopes. Unknown envelope siblings retain their located omissions;
explicit typed records in those siblings keep their original kind, ID, payload and
native mapping as well as their known aliases. The unsupported parent receives
a located warning without adding a rejected input or a fabricated vendor ID.
Untyped envelope values receive a reasoned source-only decision only after a
bounded structural check finds no nested `type` or `kind` discriminator. If an
unknown object or array wraps an explicit record at any deeper level, the whole
upload is refused at that container with `unsupported_nested_envelope`. Unwrap
the records into a documented collection before uploading. This check does not
search string values for identities and never traverses an identified record
payload as if its authors, parts or other fields were independent records. It
uses at most 4,096 nodes per opaque position and 200,000 per upload, independently
of source-position, identity-extraction and diagnostic budgets. Exhaustion
refuses the upload. The same lowering also checks saved offsets on queue resume.
This applies equally to singular fields and array items, including unknown
names and escaped JSON pointer characters.

Zendesk retains Lily's one singular wrapper per physical line, including in ZIP
members. Arrays, plural API envelopes, malformed wrappers and mixed wrappers are
refused before custody. The wrapper determines the record kind; payload fields
cannot override it. An unsupported wrapper needs a valid original source ID;
a wrapper without one is refused before it can hide nested records under an
invented outer identity. A ticket's `type` is ordinary nullable business metadata
(`problem`, `incident`, `question` or `task`). No ambiguous document can enter custody with only the
identities of one interpretation retained. These refusals also apply when the
pre-audit recovery step reindexes an old original; an unprocessable old original
therefore establishes the documented workspace/vendor fence before erasure.

Opaque fields are explicitly retained-only: `custom_attributes`, `user_fields`,
attachment metadata, Zendesk comment metadata/routing source, restrictions,
unknown workflow action values, translations and article audience/availability
metadata. Every non-null opaque value makes the index incomplete, including
strings, numbers, empty arrays and empty objects. Its contents are not mapped;
its keys and scalar values are hashed whole into the erasure index described
above. Unknown fields make the index incomplete even when their value is null. Unsupported record kinds, semantic mapping errors
and unsupported envelope collections also make the index incomplete. Unprocessable
syntax and structural limits refuse the entire upload before custody. Duplicate
JSON members (including escaped spellings of the same key) are rejected at their
source path, so ordinary JSON parsing cannot hide an earlier identity-bearing
value. Structural scanning has a maximum depth of 128.

The review reports `unsupported_source_field`, `opaque_source_field`,
`malformed_source_field` or `source_shape_limit`, with a source filename,
physical record line and a JSON pointer to the field or item. Zendesk pointers
include the singular wrapper name; JSON envelope pointers include the collection
and record index. The physical line is the beginning of the source record;
the pointer identifies a field inside a multiline record. Rejected records
retain these diagnostics too. Unrecognized or opaque values have no invented
native effect, and the private original retains their exact bytes until contact
erasure supersedes that custody.

The audit follows a fixed, acyclic schema, stops at 4,096 visited nodes per
record; exceeding that budget refuses admission. It retains at most 128 field
diagnostics plus a truncation notice, while continuing to extract every understood
identity. A presentation limit cannot hide later people or references. It
does not recurse through unknown or opaque subtrees; the erasure index hashes
their values without interpreting them. Those limits supplement
the 2 MiB upload/expanded-byte, 5,000 source-position and 128 KiB record bounds.

The temporary structural index is bounded separately from the remaining source
record count. Fields and array values within a typed record do not consume extra
source positions when that record is the final member of a multi-file export.
The complete export still refuses any position beyond its 5,000-record bound.

Encrypted, multidisk, ZIP64, unsupported compression/flags/entry types, unsafe
paths, opaque extra fields/comments and bytes outside described members are
refused with their archive or member location. Repackage source files without
extra metadata if necessary. These bytes cannot be silently retained under a
complete identity claim. Upload admission finishes all physical chunks before
R2/D1 custody or queue publication. Queue extraction uses the same validated
physical cursor on resume; directories cannot alter file identity or reuse a
previous chunk's storage keys. Pre-audit originals that fail these checks use
the documented workspace/vendor erasure fence.

Inbox v2 `_embedded` list envelopes, direct customer/conversation objects,
per-conversation thread pages and Docs v1 `items`/`article` envelopes use a
separate shape reader. The shared strict JSON scanner validates their original
syntax before extraction, including escaped duplicate member names. List
receipts remain source records and are reconciled before native mapping; embedded
chat/thread arrays do not replace per-conversation page receipts. Customer
`_embedded.emails[].value`, primary customers and thread customer/creator IDs are
indexed before private custody, including records later rejected at review.
A thread customer may have no `type`; the documented `type:customer` thread
itself determines the incoming customer role. Unread or unsupported content is
retained with source-located diagnostics and participates in the conservative
whole-value erasure index. See [Help Scout inputs](moving-in.md#help-scout-inbox-v2-and-docs-v1)
for exact grouping, pagination and publication rules.

Move in reads Zendesk `organization` wrappers and users' `organization_id`,
Freshdesk `company` wrappers and contacts' `company_id`, Intercom 2.16 typed
company records and contacts' embedded `companies` relationship, and Help Scout
organization wrappers or complete `_embedded.organizations` list responses with
customers' `organizationId`. Include those unmodified company responses alongside
the existing history export. A company name alone never creates a relationship.

Company names and explicit Zendesk/Freshdesk/Help Scout domain lists map to native
companies. Intercom's website is not a domain membership claim. Source company
IDs remain namespaced, contacts stay unverified, and company-wide portal access
stays off. Duplicate domains or a domain already owned by another native company
are review conflicts; import never merges accounts. Unsupported attributes,
sharing and routing settings are named in the review and retained in the private
original. Help Scout's checked organization shape has no source timestamps;
native creation time records the import and the omission is explicit.

Native contacts currently have one company. Zendesk's explicit default and
Freshdesk's primary company map with an omission for additional memberships;
Help Scout maps its explicit organization ID. Intercom maps only a complete
single-company relationship (`has_more: false`, matching distinct `total_count`);
multiple or incomplete relationships remain unlinked with an explicit reason.
Importing company data grants no company-wide customer history access. Later
native company or membership edits prevent whole-import undo from deleting them.

## Archive custody

Every physical ZIP member consumes an extraction position, including an empty
directory. ZIP32 stored and deflated files are supported, with optional checked
32-bit data descriptors (with or without their signature). Each member must have
matching central/local names, flags, compression, timestamps and size/CRC fields;
its decompressed size and CRC are checked before its body can be omitted. A
directory must have zero expanded bytes and a valid empty-body checksum. The
reader checks header ranges, descriptors, body ranges and nonoverlap for every
member, and decompression remains bounded by the declared and upload limits.

Encrypted, multidisk, ZIP64, unsupported compression/flags/entry types, unsafe
paths, opaque extra fields/comments and bytes outside described members are
refused with their archive or member location. Repackage source files without
extra metadata if necessary. These bytes cannot be silently retained under a
complete identity claim. Upload admission finishes all physical chunks before
R2/D1 custody or queue publication. Queue extraction uses the same validated
physical cursor on resume; directories cannot alter file identity or reuse a
previous chunk's storage keys. Pre-audit originals that fail these checks use
the documented workspace/vendor erasure fence.

# Move in your support history

Open **Settings → Move in existing support history**, or use the optional **Move in** link on the Setup page. A workspace owner or admin uploads and reviews each import. Its original files, plan and report are private to that reviewer in that workspace.

An import is inert: it does not send mail or widget messages, run AI, assign staff, activate staff access, or send notifications. Imported contacts are unverified and have no automation consent. Historical staff are retained as source authors only. Conversations solved or closed in the source land **closed**; their closing time is the source's own when the export records one, otherwise the source's last update, and the review says which. Assignment is not activated. Imported messages are history, so they never count as unread. Imported history is excluded from Reports.

Uploads are limited to 2 MiB, with at most 2 MiB of expanded source bytes, 64 ZIP entries, 5,000 source and derived-tag records and 128 KiB per record. ZIP is a packaging option for supported files. It is not a claim that either vendor's export service produces ZIP. Split larger exports into smaller complete batches, each including the contacts needed by its conversations. Keep the source files until you have checked the report.

Planning reads only candidate native identities and complete related target bundles. A persisted email index preserves Unicode comparisons and reconciles at most 100 changed native contacts per background turn; unrelated workspace history is not accumulated in memory. A native target larger than 512 KiB, or combined native candidates larger than 8 MiB, is reported as a review-size conflict before its content is loaded. Parsing indexes structural source offsets and physical lines once per file, then stages at most 100 records per batch from those saved positions. Archive extraction stages at most 20 entries per batch. One immutable review covers the whole import. Internally, reviewed plans contain at most twenty source records, 512 KiB of estimated decision material and 1 MiB of serialized plan data; an individual decision beyond that bound is refused. Large conversation bundles get a plan of their own; any record needing more than 750 native SQL writes is rejected during review with its source location. A review supports at most 300 internal plans; a larger expansion is refused before approval. Application and undo process at most twenty source records or target bundles per batch, with an additional whole-invocation D1 statement cap. Durable child journals apply in dependency order and undo in reverse order while the report shows global progress. Original uploads and extracted source bytes are retained in private object storage. The global review binds the exact original upload and parsed files by private object key, size and digest; every apply/undo invocation verifies those bytes again. Each smaller Base journal retains its reviewed decisions, source digests and provenance, and explicitly marks original bytes unavailable within that child journal. Exact bytes live in the private group custody, not duplicated in every child journal. Erasure fences the entire group before removing all child journals and source objects.

Unsupported records and fields are reported rather than turned into guessed data. Attachment metadata stays in the original unless explicitly supplied Freshdesk or offline Zendesk bytes pass the checks below. Intercom and Help Scout do not yet attach bytes to native messages. Automation, assignment rules, external actions, company and segment rules, and unsupported conversation parts are not activated. Inspect the report's source filename, physical line and JSON pointer to locate a problem. Invalid JSON, duplicate JSON members (including equivalent escaped names), invalid UTF-8, excessive nesting, oversized records, excess source positions and exhausted identity work budgets refuse the entire upload before private R2 and D1 custody or native effects. The refusal gives the source file, physical line, JSON path and reason. Every ZIP member is checked first, including directories and later extraction batches; no partial upload is retained. An export with no source records is refused after the complete bounded scan. Blank files, supported empty record lists and empty stored or deflated directories can accompany actual records, including records in later archive batches. Directories must first pass header, empty-body and checksum validation. Unsupported record kinds still count as source records and reach the reasoned plan. ZIP32 stored or deflated members and checked 32-bit data descriptors are supported. Opaque archive comments or extra fields, undeclared bytes, encrypted, multidisk or ZIP64 members and unsupported compression are refused; repackage the source files without that metadata. Correct the export and upload again. Valid JSON with unsupported kinds or mapping errors still reaches the reasoned plan; those decisions have no fabricated source ID or native effect. Input counts include repeated records and derived tags; per-kind counts describe distinct identified decisions plus invalid positions. The progress total counts only identified source decisions.

There are two ways in. **Connect Zendesk** reads the whole account for you: every ticket, archived ones included, with every comment, the people and organizations in them, ticket fields and Help Center articles. **Upload files** takes an account JSON export or packed offline files. Both go through the same review, approval, undo and erasure.

1. In Zendesk **Admin Center**, open **Apps and integrations → APIs → OAuth clients** and choose **Add OAuth client**.
   - **Name:** anything, for example *HappyToHelp move in*.
   - **Identifier:** keep the suggested one, or choose your own. You enter it in HappyToHelp.
   - **Client kind:** **Public**. Public clients use PKCE.
   - **Redirect URLs:** `<your HappyToHelp origin>/api/move-in/zendesk/callback`, for example `https://support.example.com/api/move-in/zendesk/callback`. The Move in page shows yours, ready to copy.
   - **Allowed scopes:** **read** and **hc:read** only.
2. In HappyToHelp, open **Settings → Move in existing support history**, keep **Zendesk** selected, and enter your Zendesk subdomain (`acme` for `acme.zendesk.com`) and the client's **Identifier**. Choose **Connect**. Zendesk asks a Zendesk admin to allow read access, then returns you to Move in. The full export needs an admin's connection.
3. Choose **Pull everything**. The pull runs in the background; you can leave the page. It shows what it is reading, then per kind: tickets seen, deleted in Zendesk, already imported, imported and refused; replies on imported tickets; records changed in Zendesk and kept as imported; people; organizations; and articles to publish, drafts and held back. Refused records are listed by Zendesk id with the reason.
4. When every batch is reviewed, choose **Approve and import**. That one approval covers the whole pull and binds each batch's reviewed plan. Every batch with something to import then imports by itself, one after another. A refused record never holds back the others: it stays out, listed by Zendesk id with its reason, and the rest of its batch imports. A batch whose every record was refused or is already imported has nothing to import.
5. The pull says **Pull imported** only when every record it saw is imported, already imported, kept as imported or refused with a reason. If a batch stops on the way, for example on a brief database failure or after your session ended, the pull stops too and names it. **Resume pull** continues it from its last checkpoint; a pull you stop instead is read again by the next one, which brings the stopped batch's records in as a new batch. Resume also picks up a batch that has made no progress for longer than one pull step takes, and, before approval, reviews again any batch reviewed by an earlier version of the importer, from the records it already holds, without reading Zendesk again. The pull is then ready for approval again with what this version imports.

What comes across:
- Tickets come from Zendesk's incremental ticket export, which includes archived tickets (ordinary ticket listing leaves them out). Each ticket's comments are read page by page with inline images listed. Public comments become messages and private comments become private notes, in source order with their authors.
- Deleted tickets are recorded as deleted in Zendesk. They are neither imported nor counted as refused.
- People who are end users become contacts. Agents and admins stay source authors only: no staff access is created. A person's last sign-in and last edit times are left out, so an unchanged person is recognised as the same record in a later pull.
- Customers with no email, or an email that is not a usable address (a chat visitor, say), come across as contacts with no email, recognised by their Zendesk id. Their tickets import. Such a contact is never mailed; undo and erasure remove it as they remove any imported contact.
- A ticket an agent or admin raised for themselves imports whole. Its requester comes across as an inert contact of their own: the name Zendesk holds, no email (never the staff address, never a made-up one), not verified, with no access and nothing assigned, recognised by their Zendesk id. The review names it as a staff requester imported as an inert contact. Their comments stay staff comments, and they still get no staff access. One staff member is one contact, however many tickets they raised.
- Comments Zendesk wrote itself, such as a chat transcript, come across as system messages in their place in the conversation.
- Text that only starts like a link (`http:// see below`) is read as text, not refused as a link.
- Organizations become companies. Ticket field definitions are reviewed in a batch of their own; a ticket's value for a field this importer cannot recreate stays in its source and is named in the review.
- Public published articles publish; drafts stay drafts. Articles for a restricted audience (a user segment) are held back: they create no article, category, link, search or AI answer content.
- The pull itself brings attachment and inline-image metadata only, named as an omission. Download links and their tokens are removed, and user details, queries and fragments are stripped from links before anything is stored. The files come across in a second step, **Fetch files** (below).

Files (attachments and inline images):
- Once a pull is applied, an owner or admin chooses **Fetch files** in the Zendesk panel. It uses the same Zendesk connection (no new sign-in, scope or client) and needs no approval: it changes no imported record, it only adds each file to its message or private note. One fetch runs at a time per workspace.
- It reads the comments of every Zendesk ticket the workspace holds, in ticket-id order, replies brought in by later pulls included, and fetches every attachment and inline image on a comment the workspace holds into private file storage, bound to its Zendesk attachment id and its comment. A file on a public comment shows on that message to the team and the conversation's customer; a file on a private comment shows on its private note to the team only and never reaches the customer. Files download byte-exact through the conversation's file link; no other workspace and no signed-out request can download them. Any file type is kept, up to Zendesk's 50 MB maximum; only passive types open in the browser, everything else downloads.
- Hosts: each file is requested first from your own `https://SUBDOMAIN.zendesk.com` address, the only place the Zendesk sign-in is sent. Zendesk answers with a temporary link; redirects are followed by hand, at most three, and only to your own `https://SUBDOMAIN.zendesk.com` or `https://SUBDOMAIN.zdusercontent.com`, without the sign-in. A file whose link or redirect points anywhere else is not fetched and that host is never contacted. No sign-in, link, temporary link or redirect target is stored or logged; stopped runs and refusals carry codes only.
- Refusals are listed by attachment id with their ticket id and reason: a file deleted in Zendesk, one Zendesk flagged as malware, one whose link points outside your account, one larger than 50 MB, or one Zendesk answered with an error. A ticket the workspace holds that Zendesk no longer returns is listed by ticket id. Nothing is skipped silently.
- It runs in small background steps, each saving where it is. Each file is streamed into storage with its known size and never held whole in memory, so a file up to Zendesk's 50 MB maximum fits; one whose download is shorter or longer than its size is not kept and is listed by id. Zendesk's `Retry-After` (on 429, and on 503 when given) is honoured by scheduling the next step, never by waiting in place. A database failure, a Zendesk sign-in that needs renewing, or a member who can no longer act stops it with the reason. So does a background step that died partway, or one that never ran: once a step's time has passed with nothing saved, the fetch shows as stopped partway, never sooner. **Resume** (by any owner or admin, whose session then carries it) continues from where it stopped, without reading again the tickets it had finished. **Fetch what is left** is offered after a stop as well as once a fetch is done: it starts a new fetch in place of the stopped one, reads every ticket again, brings files on new comments and tries refused files again, and never downloads a file already stored. Files supplied in an offline export count as stored.
- The counts and the list of files not fetched cover only comments the workspace still holds. When undo removes a reply or private note (one with no fetched file), its files leave the counts and the list at once.
- Undo of a batch whose conversation has fetched files keeps that conversation as edited here, as for a file an agent uploaded. The same holds for a reply or private note a later pull brought in: once it has a fetched file, undoing that pull's batch keeps it as edited here, stops with a conflict and removes nothing. Erasing a contact removes their conversations' files with their bytes.
- An import is inert, as above: nothing is sent, assigned, notified or answered by AI, and imported history stays out of Reports.

Limits and pace:
- A batch is an ordinary Move in import of at most 2 MiB and 5,000 records, carrying the people, organizations and field definitions its tickets need. A ticket imports whole as one conversation in one import, up to 960 KiB of cleaned JSON and 750 native rows (about 370 public or 745 private comments). A larger ticket is refused by id with its reason; it is never split, shortened or dropped silently. Uploaded files keep their 2 MiB and 128 KiB-per-record limits.
- Zendesk allows 10 incremental export requests a minute; the pull keeps to that and waits as long as Zendesk's `Retry-After` asks. Waiting is scheduled, not slept. A Zendesk refusal of the incremental export (HTTP 403) stops the pull with that reason; nothing is read another way.
- The sign-in is renewed shortly before it expires (access lasts up to 48 hours, renewal up to 90 days). If Zendesk refuses the renewal, Move in shows **Reconnect Zendesk** and does not retry by itself.
- Pulling again later (**Pull new and changed history**) starts where the last applied pull stopped, so it reads only tickets, people and organizations that are new or changed in Zendesk. New tickets import as new conversations. Each Zendesk id still maps to one conversation, and records already imported and unchanged are left as they are.
- New replies on a ticket that is already imported come across: each Zendesk comment the conversation does not yet have imports as a reply of its own, keyed by its Zendesk comment id, at the end of that conversation (public comments as messages, private comments as private notes). The conversation itself is not rewritten.
- A ticket, person or organization that changed in Zendesk after it was imported (a new status, subject, assignee or tags; a new name or email) is kept as imported. The pull counts it under **changed in Zendesk, kept as imported** and never refuses it for that. New tickets and replies from a changed person link to that person's existing contact, and a changed organization stays the company it was. Only a record that is new and cannot be imported is refused. A changed ticket field definition or article is still refused by id (`source_changed_conflict`); the rest of its batch imports.
- Undoing a pulled batch takes out what it imported, replies included. The next pull then reads the whole account again from the start: everything the undo took out imports again, and everything still held is recognised and left as it is.
- Any owner or admin of the workspace can pull. One pull runs at a time for the workspace, and every owner and admin sees it on the Move in page. The member who started it approves it and resumes it after a stop. A workspace owner can also stop another member's pull before it is approved, or take over one that stopped (or whose member can no longer act) with **Take over pull**: it then reads Zendesk again under the owner's name, and what the other member's batches already hold stays as their imports. An approved pull keeps importing under the member who approved it; if it stops, or that member can no longer act (removed from the workspace, say), a workspace owner can **Stop this pull**: what it imported stays, and the next pull imports the rest. The next pull by any owner or admin starts where the last applied pull stopped, whoever ran it.
- One workspace holds one Zendesk account. Once it holds Zendesk history, connecting a different subdomain is refused; use another workspace for another account.
- **Disconnect** removes the stored sign-in and asks Zendesk to revoke it, reporting Zendesk's answer. If Zendesk does not revoke it, remove the OAuth client in Admin Center.
- Hosted pulls need the Workers Paid plan's D1 budget, as every import does.

Use the documented [account JSON export](https://support.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/4408886165402-Exporting-data-to-a-JSON-CSV-or-XML-file), with one singular wrapped object per nonblank line, for example `{"user":{...}}` or `{"ticket":{...}}`. Ticket records must contain the complete comments array; a ticket description is not a substitute. Include the users needed to identify requesters and comment authors. Each comment needs its source ID, original creation timestamp and explicit `public` boolean. Public comments become messages; private comments become private notes.
Saved replies and Help Center articles are separate API supplements, not part of a claim that the account export contains every supported kind:

Upload the resulting file through **Move in → Zendesk → Upload and review**.
The packer reads local files only, makes no network requests and never writes
native state. It accepts source JSON arrays, objects with `tickets`, `users` or
`organizations` arrays, `ticket_fields` supplements, and singular wrapped JSONL/NDJSON records. Split account
members can appear in any order. Unpacked uploads retain the existing singular
wrapper-per-line format; arbitrary account JSON collections require this packing
step. ZIP uploads may contain multiple such wrapped files, within the same limits.

The manifest is local packing metadata, not a Zendesk export schema. Paths are
relative to its directory; absolute paths, parent traversal, symlinks and files
outside that directory are refused. For example:

Here the local file contains exactly `hello`. Its corresponding Zendesk comment
attachment must have `id:501`, `file_name`, `content_type` and `size:5`. Zendesk's
`content_url` is metadata, never a download instruction. Duplicate filenames are
fine; attachment IDs and local paths must have exactly one owner. The packer removes attachment download URLs entirely, including path-based
access tokens, and strips user information, queries and fragments from other
URL values before output; direct uploads with
credential-bearing links are refused before custody. Direct Zendesk attachment
URL metadata with any query, fragment or credential path is refused as well; pack it locally to
strip those access-bearing parts first. Original local files are not
uploaded by this command. Preserve them privately yourself when appropriate.

Comments files hold a `comments` array (or an array of comments), associated with
the manifest's explicit `ticket_id`. Supply every page, numbered from 1 through
`pages`, each marked `complete:true` only after reconciling it; a non-null
`next_page`, a missing page, source `comments_truncated`/`comments_incomplete`,
or a mismatched `comment_count` makes the ticket visibly incomplete and rejects
it in review. Supplied comments replace the ticket's embedded array. Without a
separate file, the embedded complete array remains supported. A description
never replaces missing comments. Identical repeated tickets reach the mounted review as exact repeated records and are counted once; differing
copies require correction before packing. Conflicting IDs in direct uploads
remain source-located review rejections.

Metric files hold `ticket_metric_events`; audit files hold `audits`. Each record
joins by its original `ticket_id`; for a per-ticket response that omits it, set
`ticket_id` on that manifest file. Empty event files can declare that ticket ID
to distinguish supplied-empty from missing history. Event IDs, instance IDs,
metric names, timestamps, audit status transitions, source targets and supplied
elapsed units remain inert private history. Unknown event types stay labeled as
unsupported. Privacy/redaction audit events are unsupported and refuse the ticket. Use a
separately reconciled supported conversation export; old text is never treated
as the redacted version.
Missing files stay unavailable; current status never supplies an invented SLA
result. Staff with current ticket access open **Details → Summary → Imported
status and SLA history**. Customers cannot read this private history.

Packing enrichments live only under a ticket's `_offline` object, identified by
`format:happytohelp-zendesk-offline-v1`: `attachments` binds `attachment_id`,
`comment_id`, relative `path`, `sha256` and canonical `base64`; `history` declares
`metrics` and `audits` as `missing` or `supplied`; `metric_events`, `audits` and
`provenance` retain their source file, digest, row and JSON pointer. These are
explicit local packing fields, never required fields in an untouched Zendesk
export. The review identifies packed file/row/pointer and source ticket ID;
provenance retains the original component locations inside private ticket custody.
Packed users, organizations and field definitions carry the same file/digest/row/pointer
as a list under `_offline_provenance`, retained in their guarded native source provenance.
The exact packed bytes bind the reviewed fingerprint.

Supplied bytes use the existing native media store and access rules, at most
48 KiB per file and 20 supplied files per ticket. Public comments keep public
attachments; internal notes keep teammate-only attachments. Types and bounds
match Freshdesk. URL-only attachments are visible omissions, never binary
successes. Digest, size or ownership mismatches reject the entire ticket before
native effects. Inert history is part of the native adapter's guarded
`move_in_origins.source_json`, its plans, repeat/undo and portable database;
there is no separate history store. Erasure removes the affected custody and
bytes and keeps source-identity replay fences.

Keep each packed upload and its decoded input within 2 MiB, each ticket with its
history and bytes within 128 KiB, and source plus derived records within 5,000.
Larger exports need separate manifest batches of complete tickets, each including
their users, organizations, field definitions and relevant history. Do not split
one ticket's conversation across independent imports. A complete ticket beyond
128 KiB cannot be imported by this bounded slice. Full configuration fidelity,
shared M3 opt-in/Business grants/catch-up transport, signed real-export
qualification, other vendors and final live cutover remain unproved.

**Settings → Cutover** (linked from Move in) is where a workspace records switching each source over: **Zendesk**, **Legacy HappyToHelp**, the **Email route** and the **Website widget**. The switch itself happens in your own tools, made by you or by your agent. Cutover only keeps the record, so nobody keeps notes anywhere else, and it calls nothing: reading it sends no request to any provider, queues no job and sends no mail. A workspace owner or admin can open it, and so can a custom role that holds the data import permission; the Agent role and collaborators cannot.

Each source shows where it stands: **With the old tool** (before any step), **Switched here** (this workspace takes the work) or **Old tool retired** (the old tool takes no more of it). The state is the newest recorded step's. Under it are the live counts, read from this workspace's own records each time the page loads, and every recorded step, newest first: what changed, when and by whom, the check result with its detail, and how to undo it.

- **Zendesk** counts the conversations Move in imported from Zendesk that are still in the workspace (uploads and pulls, so an undone import drops out), and names when the newest applied pull finished with the tickets and replies it imported.
- **Legacy HappyToHelp** counts the conversations a legacy import mapped into the workspace and names when the newest completed legacy sweep that carried them finished.
- **Email route** counts mail delivered into the workspace, and **Website widget** the conversations a visitor started through the widget and wrote in. Both count from the latest of the last Zendesk pull, the last legacy sweep and that source's own newest step. A source with none of these counts from the start. Mail and widget conversations that arrive after a switch are the sign that work is reaching this workspace; arrivals that keep landing at the old tool show there instead.

**Record a step** opens a short form: the source, the state after the step, what changed, how to undo it, the check result (passed, failed or not run) and its detail. An agent records the same step with `POST /api/move-in/projects/PROJECT_ID/cutover/steps`, signed in as an owner or admin as it does for a Zendesk pull:

`change` and `undo` are required text of at most 2,000 characters, and `check.detail` is optional. The server records the time and the signed-in member; the request cannot set them. A step is never edited or deleted. To undo a switch, record a newer step (for example `"state":"incumbent"` with what was restored): the source's state follows the newest step. Each recorded step also writes one event to the security log. `GET /api/move-in/projects/PROJECT_ID/cutover` returns the four sources exactly as the page shows them. See [the API guide](api.md#move-in-zendesk-connection-and-pull).

The simplest route needs only an Intercom access token: **Settings → Project →
Move in → Intercom** shows a Terminal script that reads every conversation and
its contacts from the [Conversations API](https://developers.intercom.com/docs/references/rest-api/api.intercom.io/conversations/conversation)
(`Intercom-Version: 2.16`) and writes `intercom-move-in-1.jsonl`, `-2` and so
on, 25 conversations each, with each conversation's contacts on lines before
it. A conversation with more than 500 parts is longer than the API returns at
once; its count no longer matches its parts and the review lists it as rejected.

Use the [conversation cloud export](https://www.intercom.com/help/en/articles/7029721-export-conversations-data-to-amazon-s3) configured for Data API **2.16**, in JSON or JSONL. The reader also accepts a top-level JSON array and convenience `contacts`/`conversations` arrays. ZIP may package these files and separate API supplements. Reporting CSV, macro-content CSV, PDF, text and NDJSON are unsupported.

Include [Contacts API](https://developers.intercom.com/docs/references/rest-api/api.intercom.io/contacts) records for the single contact referenced by each conversation. A contact needs its original ID, valid email and Unix creation time. Conversation channel must be explicit in `channel.initial` (`email` or `messenger`), state must be `open`, `closed` or `snoozed`, and the conversation parts must be complete. When supplied, `conversation_parts.total_count` must be a nonnegative safe integer exactly equal to the supplied parts array length; malformed counts and mismatches are rejected. Comments become visible messages; notes remain private. Source authors retain their exported type and identity. Contact tags remain contact metadata; conversation tags become workspace tags. Duplicate contact or conversation IDs are reported as conflicts.

The initial conversation source has no documented message creation timestamp. Its displayed time is explicitly **conversation creation time**, with the original message timestamp recorded as unavailable. Part timestamps remain their original Unix timestamps. No message timestamp is fabricated.

- [Macros 2.16](https://developers.intercom.com/docs/references/rest-api/api.intercom.io/macros/macro): `type: "macro"`, `id`, `name`, body, ISO8601 creation/update strings, `visible_to: "everyone"`, and an `available_on` list containing `inbox`. Team-restricted macros are rejected. Both original HTML and plain text are inspected before conversion. Dynamic placeholders, including XML-like `<attribute>` elements and their fallback values, are rejected explicitly because native saved replies cannot preserve their behavior. The API's `{type:"list",data:[...]}` envelope is accepted. Unsupported sibling collections and unknown fields receive source-located omissions; their records count in the review.
- [Articles](https://developers.intercom.com/docs/references/rest-api/api.intercom.io/articles): `type: "article"`, source ID, title, body, Unix creation/update times and explicit `state: "published"` or `"draft"`. Unsupported audience restrictions are rejected. Publication state is preserved. HTML is converted to native Markdown; a provided article `body_markdown` is preserved.

Choose **Freshdesk** in Move in. The page gives a script that uses the [Freshdesk API v2](https://developers.freshdesk.com/api/) with your API key (your profile picture, **Profile settings**, **Your API Key**). It writes `freshdesk-move-in-1.ndjson`, `-2` and so on, 50 tickets each, plus `freshdesk-move-in-saved-replies.ndjson`. Upload them one at a time.

- The ticket description becomes the first message, from the requester, at the ticket's creation time. An outbound-email ticket (`source` 10) was written by an agent Freshdesk does not record, so that first message has no named author.
- Public replies become messages; private notes (`private: true`) stay private notes. Messages keep their original times and authors.
- Resolved (4) and closed (5) tickets, and spam, land closed. The closing time is `stats.closed_at` or `stats.resolved_at`, else the ticket's last update. Open (2), pending (3) and custom statuses stay open. Assignment is not activated.
- Agents stay as the authors of their messages and get no access. Contacts need a valid email; extra addresses (`other_emails`) are kept for erasure matching but not imported.
- Canned responses visible to all agents (`visibility` 0) become saved replies. Personal or group responses, and responses with placeholders such as `{{ticket.requester.name}}`, are rejected.
- Metadata-only attachments keep their names and sizes in your original file; the files themselves stay in Freshdesk. Freshdesk's attachment and avatar links contain signed keys, which an import must not keep, so the script removes them and an upload that still has one is refused with its line. The script also leaves out email address lists (to, cc, from) and empty custom fields; other custom fields stay in your original file.

In the singular-wrapped Freshdesk NDJSON format above, add `base64` and `sha256` to each attachment object in the ticket's `attachments` array or a conversation part's `attachments` array. Supply the bytes yourself; the importer never downloads a URL. The export script does not fetch attachment bytes. For example, the UTF-8 bytes `hello` are:

Review shows filenames, digests and the source visibility before approval. Ticket-level attachments belong to the opening message; public conversation-part attachments belong to that message; private attachments belong to that private note. Private-note attachments are available only to teammates with ticket access, never to customer sessions. Small imported payloads are retained in native database storage with the media row, inside the same guarded transaction as their owning message or note. Resume and repeat preserve that ownership. Undo removes unchanged attachment rows and bytes together; any later native attachment edit stops undo. Contact erasure removes the payloads and import custody and fences replay. This bounded format does not establish other-vendor attachments, live cutover or outbound attachment delivery.

Uploading again is safe. A rejected record is not imported and does not hold its source ID, so fix it in your file and upload the corrected file: records already imported are recognised and left as they are, and only the fixed record is added. An import made by an earlier release kept a rejected record's ID; the review then says so, and undoing that earlier import releases it. Uploading the identical completed export again reports that every record is already imported. It performs no application-row mutations, including import bookkeeping. D1 platform read metadata can still change. Under the owner decision of 2026-10-09, repeat and undo compare exact business state; only platform counters/sequences, audit and import journals are excluded. Changed source records, deleted imported targets and native target collisions are shown as conflicts for review. Native deletion is preserved. Applying a review checks the complete reviewed contact identity set again inside each publishing transaction, including case-insensitive email matches and intervening native identity changes; a collision stops publication until it is resolved. A collision present before the first publishing transaction prevents initial publication. If a collision arrives between committed batches, the refused transaction publishes nothing and the report retains the exact committed progress. Resume rechecks the conflict; **Undo whole import** can reverse unchanged records from a stopped import while preserving the competing native contact. Current target contents are also checked atomically.

**Undo whole import** removes unchanged records created by that import, in reverse dependency order. Original files and provenance remain available in the private import journal. A later native edit, note, or reference from another conversation blocks reversal with a conflict and is preserved; undo does not overwrite it. Opening history does not block undo: read markers for removed imported conversations are removed with them. Pre-existing native records and their read markers remain intact.

Contact erasure takes precedence over import custody. If an archive contains the erased contact, its original bytes, staged records and import journal are removed. This also applies to ordinary native contacts when staged source identities match a known email or external identity, including records rejected during review. Embedded source-author email aliases are indexed too. Malformed identity fields, malformed contact collections and unknown or opaque source fields make the identity index incomplete. Every whole value in those fields is hashed into a private index, so erasure removes such an import only when it holds the erased contact's email, external ID or source ID, or a known alias, and leaves other people's imports in place. Erasure retains the original identity and its complete known alias closure in its first transaction. If a native identity changed before that transaction, a bounded retry retains both snapshots; it also fences any identity seen after the committed transaction. Interrupted erasure keeps these hash-only fences, and concurrent native updates cannot overwrite the erasure state. After an erasure, an upload with an incomplete identity index is refused rather than retaining source bytes whose identity cannot be checked. Because a mixed archive is indivisible, that whole import and any import journals depending on its reused decisions become **Source erased** and cannot be resumed, replayed or undone. Other native records from that import remain in the workspace. The retained artifact digest prevents replay of the erased file. Hash-only identity fences also prevent differently packaged or changed exports from restoring a known erased source identity, requester or author. No erased email, external ID or source ID is stored as plaintext in those fences. Uploads index these identities before private custody is admitted. This admission scan shares the 2 MiB expanded-byte, 5,000-position and 128 KiB per-record limits; unsupported semantic identity shapes mark the index incomplete, while any exceeded structural or identity scan limit refuses upload before custody. Structural indexing refuses the upload when its position budget is reached. Identity extraction permits at most 4,096 schema nodes per record, 200,000 per upload, 40,000 identity hashes and 20,000 distinct identity links. Its 128 field diagnostics plus one truncation notice are a separate presentation budget: all understood aliases are indexed even after that notice. The upload route measures separately from the queued parser and remains subject to local capacity checks; local request duration does not establish hosted CPU usage. The route checks the identity fence atomically when recording the upload. Each object uses a unique opaque conditional write reservation so an in-flight writer cannot restore content after erasure deletes its key. If an upload is interrupted before it reaches background processing, upload the same file again to finish that reserved upload.

Records with an explicit type keep that meaning even when additional fields
have collection names or an unknown envelope property contains the record.
The original kind, ID, payload and native mapping survive such a parent; the
unsupported parent is reported at its source position. Conflicting record/list declarations, malformed record
discriminators and ambiguous wrappers are refused with a source location before
any private file or import is saved. JSON, JSONL and ZIP packaging use the same
record classification for review and erasure protection. Unknown envelope
containers that hide an explicit record under additional object or array layers
are refused as a whole at that container. Unwrap those records into a documented
collection. The bounded structural check examines discriminator keys, never
searches message text for identities, and preserves the payload boundary of an
identified record.

The [source-structure and erasure reference](moving-in-shapes.md) lists the
understood nested containers, nullable fields, opaque values and bounded audit
behavior. Field diagnostics carry the physical record line and exact JSON
pointer, including fields on rejected records. Unsupported structural content
cannot claim a complete custody index merely because its enclosing record maps.

These readers, including Freshdesk, have synthetic fixture coverage. The committed deterministic generator provides separate clean and malformed/duplicate 1,000-conversation corpora for each vendor. The capacity harness exercises upload, reviewed import, repeat and native undo in the native local Worker/D1/R2 runtime. It retains full ordered table snapshots and separately measures the protected D1 read counter. Repeat and undo must preserve exact business state, including private notes, tags, source-linked content and all other imported business rows. Only named platform counters/sequences, audit and import journals are excluded. Hash receipts cover those full ordered business snapshots; synthetic credential material is not written to evidence. Sampled used JavaScript heap peaks remain below 128 MiB after bounded child processing; the test records all available numeric isolate memory fields. These samples can miss peaks and do not measure total Worker memory. Local workerd does not enforce the deployed isolate memory limit, so this does not establish hosted memory acceptance. Real customer exports have not been supplied; this is documented-format, synthetic-only validation. It is not a claim of verified compatibility with every export variation.

The reader behavior is based on the pinned Lily Zendesk parser (`d24f3f7`) and Beacon Intercom parser (`fa1846b`), supplemented by the official API documents linked above. The shared import engine is copied byte-for-byte from the Base revision and paths recorded in `edition.json`; the product supplies its readers, native mappings, authority checks and UI. The selected D1 dependency closure excludes optional Node SQLite and HTTP-reader implementations.

Older originals from before the admission audit are reindexed from their actual private bytes before erasure removes them. At most two originals are checked per erasure request; a continuation response asks the owner to repeat erasure when more remain. The migration preserves native rows and conservatively clears old completeness claims. If an old original is missing, corrupted or outside the bounded audit, native erasure still completes and removes its custody. Future imports of that format in that workspace are then refused because the destroyed original cannot establish its missing aliases. This compatibility restriction applies only to unprocessable pre-audit custody; new uploads cannot enter that state.

The platform admission index's `move_in_contact_keys.email_digest` is lazy,
derived memoization. Business equality retains its exact project/contact links
and independently validates each populated digest against the native email;
NULL-to-correct-digest does not change business state. The contact row, email,
identity and every source/business link remain in the equality comparison.

The 9 October Base refresh requires additive migration
`118_import_kit_runtime.sql` before starting the updated Worker. Preserve the
previous 50 migration files and back up journals, identity tombstones and private
source objects together. This supplies the current official runtime dependency
schema; it does not expose new streaming or staging import workflows.

All grouping uses the same syntax, identity and size admission checks.

Published customer messages and replies become native messages; published
`type:note` threads become private notes. `draft`, `bounced`, `hidden`, `review`
and `underreview` threads are explicitly omitted from native sent history.
Unknown states and unsupported public thread kinds reject the conversation;
line-item events remain metadata. Attachments retain metadata, not downloaded
bytes. A thread's `savedReplyId` is only a reference: this format does **not**
claim to import saved replies. Unsupported fields and records appear in review.

Docs accepts [collection](https://developer.helpscout.com/docs-api/collections/list/)
and [category](https://developer.helpscout.com/docs-api/categories/list/) list

categories, their categories become children, and article/category links are

identify the request's `draft` flag, `hasDraft:true` is ambiguous and is imported
only as a draft, even when its status says `published`. Keep separately fetched
draft bodies in `articleDrafts`; they never enter the public help center.

A Zendesk file can also contain singular `group`, `view`, `schedule`, `trigger` and `automation` records. Include complete original timestamps. Groups import without members or a new default. Views with supported all-conditions import privately for the importing admin. Schedules retain supported weekly intervals, timezone and explicit holiday date ranges but start inactive. Supported triggers and hourly automations become native drafts: review the per-item changes, open their native settings from the import report, preview, then publish explicitly. Unsupported rule conditions or actions set the whole rule aside; a missing condition is never dropped to broaden a rule. Native rules process new journal events, and hourly automations run once per matching ticket episode. Broader SLA policies, memberships, defaults, brands and other vendors’ configuration equivalents remain incomplete.

New imports retain their explicit lifecycle and channel. Zendesk/Freshdesk distinguish final Closed from Solved; Help Scout/Intercom use a reopenable Closed state, which maps to native Solved. Historical owners are not granted native access or activated. Existing imported records are not rewritten when this mapping changes: a changed mapping meeting earlier native state remains a review conflict.

After import, review the ownership page and explicitly map the recorded historical owners and groups to current workspace members and groups. The chosen owner must still belong to the chosen group when activation applies; changed import authority or membership requires a fresh review. Activation preserves the requester and lifecycle, grants no historical staff access and sends no notifications. Help Scout records one assignee, either a user or a team, so its source does not provide both assignments on one ticket. Older imports without assignment snapshots remain unactivated; historical ownership is never guessed.

Upload a singular `sla_policy` wrapper alongside its singular `schedule` record.
This slice accepts exactly one `policy_metrics` entry: `metric` is
`first_reply_time`, `business_hours` is `true`, `target` is positive business
minutes, and `priority` is explicitly `low`, `normal`, `high` or `urgent`.
Other priorities receive no commitment from this policy. The source `filter` must have
empty `any` and either empty `all` or only matching `priority is` conditions.
Extra metrics, other conditions, unknown semantics and conflicting schedules
reject the entire policy; no condition or metric is discarded to widen scope.

Zendesk policy exports do not establish a calendar association. After reviewing
the source schedule, the importing admin must add `move_in_schedule_id` with
that schedule's source ID to the policy payload. This is a Move in annotation,
not a Zendesk API field. The schedule must be present and supported in the same
upload. Review the named association and priority in the upload preview before
approving. No account default or calendar is inferred.

bundle inside the existing 2 MiB, 5,000-record and 128 KiB-per-ticket limits.

The existing owner/admin Move in upload, review, apply and undo doors remain.

Well-formed Zendesk articles with boolean `draft` and an explicit restricted

Inbox search accepts the exact original Zendesk ticket ID, with or without `#`,

Erasure withdraws door upload, snapshot and archive custody and fences same or

Uploads are limited to 2 MiB, with at most 2 MiB of expanded source bytes, 64 ZIP entries, 5,000 source and derived-tag records and 128 KiB per record. ZIP is a packaging option for supported files. It is not a claim that either vendor's export service produces ZIP. Split larger exports into smaller complete batches, each including the contacts needed by its conversations. Keep the source files until you have checked the report.

Planning reads only candidate native identities and complete related target bundles. A persisted email index preserves Unicode comparisons and reconciles at most 100 changed native contacts per background turn; unrelated workspace history is not accumulated in memory. A native target larger than 512 KiB, or combined native candidates larger than 8 MiB, is reported as a review-size conflict before its content is loaded. Parsing indexes structural source offsets and physical lines once per file, then stages at most 100 records per batch from those saved positions. Archive extraction stages at most 20 entries per batch. One immutable review covers the whole import. Internally, reviewed plans contain at most twenty source records, 512 KiB of estimated decision material and 1 MiB of serialized plan data; an individual decision beyond that bound is refused. Large conversation bundles get a plan of their own; any record needing more than 750 native SQL writes is rejected during review with its source location. A review supports at most 300 internal plans; a larger expansion is refused before approval. Application and undo process at most twenty source records or target bundles per batch, with an additional whole-invocation D1 statement cap. Durable child journals apply in dependency order and undo in reverse order while the report shows global progress. Original uploads and extracted source bytes are retained in private object storage. The global review binds the exact original upload and parsed files by private object key, size and digest; every apply/undo invocation verifies those bytes again. Each smaller Base journal retains its reviewed decisions, source digests and provenance, and explicitly marks original bytes unavailable within that child journal. Exact bytes live in the private group custody, not duplicated in every child journal. Erasure fences the entire group before removing all child journals and source objects.

Unsupported records and fields are reported rather than turned into guessed data. Attachment metadata stays in the original unless explicitly supplied Freshdesk or offline Zendesk bytes pass the checks below. Intercom and Help Scout do not yet attach bytes to native messages. Automation, assignment rules, external actions, company and segment rules, and unsupported conversation parts are not activated. Inspect the report's source filename, physical line and JSON pointer to locate a problem. Invalid JSON, duplicate JSON members (including equivalent escaped names), invalid UTF-8, excessive nesting, oversized records, excess source positions and exhausted identity work budgets refuse the entire upload before private R2 and D1 custody or native effects. The refusal gives the source file, physical line, JSON path and reason. Every ZIP member is checked first, including directories and later extraction batches; no partial upload is retained. An export with no source records is refused after the complete bounded scan. Blank files, supported empty record lists and empty stored or deflated directories can accompany actual records, including records in later archive batches. Directories must first pass header, empty-body and checksum validation. Unsupported record kinds still count as source records and reach the reasoned plan. ZIP32 stored or deflated members and checked 32-bit data descriptors are supported. Opaque archive comments or extra fields, undeclared bytes, encrypted, multidisk or ZIP64 members and unsupported compression are refused; repackage the source files without that metadata. Correct the export and upload again. Valid JSON with unsupported kinds or mapping errors still reaches the reasoned plan; those decisions have no fabricated source ID or native effect. Input counts include repeated records and derived tags; per-kind counts describe distinct identified decisions plus invalid positions. The progress total counts only identified source decisions.

There are two ways in. **Connect Zendesk** reads the whole account for you: every ticket, archived ones included, with every comment, the people and organizations in them, ticket fields and Help Center articles. **Upload files** takes an account JSON export or packed offline files. Both go through the same review, approval, undo and erasure.

Limits and pace:
- A batch is an ordinary Move in import of at most 2 MiB and 5,000 records, carrying the people, organizations and field definitions its tickets need. A ticket imports whole as one conversation in one import, up to 960 KiB of cleaned JSON and 750 native rows (about 370 public or 745 private comments). A larger ticket is refused by id with its reason; it is never split, shortened or dropped silently. Uploaded files keep their 2 MiB and 128 KiB-per-record limits.
- Zendesk allows 10 incremental export requests a minute; the pull keeps to that and waits as long as Zendesk's `Retry-After` asks. Waiting is scheduled, not slept. A Zendesk refusal of the incremental export (HTTP 403) stops the pull with that reason; nothing is read another way.
- The sign-in is renewed shortly before it expires (access lasts up to 48 hours, renewal up to 90 days). If Zendesk refuses the renewal, Move in shows **Reconnect Zendesk** and does not retry by itself.
- Pulling again later (**Pull new and changed history**) starts where the last applied pull stopped, so it reads only tickets, people and organizations that are new or changed in Zendesk. New tickets import as new conversations. Each Zendesk id still maps to one conversation, and records already imported and unchanged are left as they are.
- New replies on a ticket that is already imported come across: each Zendesk comment the conversation does not yet have imports as a reply of its own, keyed by its Zendesk comment id, at the end of that conversation (public comments as messages, private comments as private notes). The conversation itself is not rewritten.
- A ticket, person or organization that changed in Zendesk after it was imported (a new status, subject, assignee or tags; a new name or email) is kept as imported. The pull counts it under **changed in Zendesk, kept as imported** and never refuses it for that. New tickets and replies from a changed person link to that person's existing contact, and a changed organization stays the company it was. Only a record that is new and cannot be imported is refused. A changed ticket field definition or article is still refused by id (`source_changed_conflict`); the rest of its batch imports.
- Undoing a pulled batch takes out what it imported, replies included. The next pull then reads the whole account again from the start: everything the undo took out imports again, and everything still held is recognised and left as it is.
- Any owner or admin of the workspace can pull. One pull runs at a time for the workspace, and every owner and admin sees it on the Move in page. The member who started it approves it and resumes it after a stop. A workspace owner can also stop another member's pull before it is approved, or take over one that stopped (or whose member can no longer act) with **Take over pull**: it then reads Zendesk again under the owner's name, and what the other member's batches already hold stays as their imports. An approved pull keeps importing under the member who approved it; if it stops, or that member can no longer act (removed from the workspace, say), a workspace owner can **Stop this pull**: what it imported stays, and the next pull imports the rest. The next pull by any owner or admin starts where the last applied pull stopped, whoever ran it.
- One workspace holds one Zendesk account. Once it holds Zendesk history, connecting a different subdomain is refused; use another workspace for another account.
- **Disconnect** removes the stored sign-in and asks Zendesk to revoke it, reporting Zendesk's answer. If Zendesk does not revoke it, remove the OAuth client in Admin Center.
- Hosted pulls need the Workers Paid plan's D1 budget, as every import does.

Ticket records must contain the complete comments array; a ticket description is not a substitute. Include the users needed to identify requesters and comment authors. Choose **Freshdesk** in Move in. The page gives a script that uses the [Freshdesk API v2](https://developers.freshdesk.com/api/) with your API key (your profile picture, **Profile settings**, **Your API Key**). It writes `freshdesk-move-in-1.ndjson`, `-2` and so on, 50 tickets each, plus `freshdesk-move-in-saved-replies.ndjson`. Upload them one at a time.

In the singular-wrapped Freshdesk NDJSON format above, add `base64` and `sha256` to each attachment object in the ticket's `attachments` array or a conversation part's `attachments` array.
